zh.question: 土星旁边大小不同的卫星，绕完一圈的时间会一样吗？
zh.observe: 打开太阳系中的土星卫星视图，让轨道示意运行；依次选择土卫一和土卫六，比较公转周期与直径读数。再阅读土卫六、土卫二的发现说明，区分屏幕标记、实际尺寸与探测器证据。

academic.title: 共同引力场中的不同轨道
academic.body: 在土星质量占主导、忽略摄动的近似下，卫星周期满足T²≈4π²a³/(GM)，轨道半长轴越大，周期通常越长。画面让七颗所选卫星共享时间推进，但为了看清轨道压缩了距离、放大了天体。真实系统还包含共振、偏心和倾角变化；轨道线不是可见的物质环，卫星也不是挂在土星环上的珠子。

academic.title: 同为卫星也有不同世界
academic.body: 土卫六拥有浓厚的以氮为主的大气，表面已确认存在甲烷和乙烷组成的湖海，其液体循环并不等于地球的水循环。土卫二的冰壳下有全球海洋，南极附近裂隙喷出水汽与冰粒。卡西尼通过成像、光谱和粒子测量研究这些环境；有液态水和有机物不等于已经发现生命。

academic.title: 用直径读数比较大小
academic.body: 选择一颗卫星，说明区会给出公转周期与直径。大小比较应使用这些带单位的直径读数：轨道图中的球体和距离分别调整，不能把屏幕上的圆球直径当作同一长度比例的测量。土卫六的实际直径远大于土卫二。七颗是教学选择，不是土星卫星总数；完整目录与数量统计需要来源和更新时间。

zh.misconception: 土星不只有七颗卫星；本页挑选七颗做比较。土卫六的湖海不是液态水，土卫二喷流也不是已经发现生物的证据。
zh.boundary: 轨道采用圆周与示意相位，球体大小和轨道距离分别调整。当前视图用简化球体标记卫星；大气、海洋与南极喷流属于探测器发现的文字说明，不是图中可近观的表面或喷流模拟。没有共同真实比例的卫星大小工作台，比较尺寸应读直径数值。

narration.label: 光环外的伙伴
narration.text: 土星有漂亮的光环，旁边还有许多卫星。今天先认识其中七颗，并不是它只有七颗。它们有的大，有的小，有的离土星近，有的离得远。先选中一颗，看清它的名字，再在画面里找到它，这样就不会跟丢啦。
narration.cue: 显示轨道全景并选中土卫六。

narration.label: 谁先绕完一圈
narration.text: 让卫星继续绕行，比较靠里的土卫一和远一些的土卫六。先暂停猜一猜：同样一段播放时间，谁会多绕几圈？再选中它们，读一读公转周期。你会发现，卫星虽然围着同一个土星，却不是排好队、用一样的速度前进，每个世界都有自己的节奏。
narration.cue: 比较土卫一与土卫六；停顿约四秒。

narration.label: 两种特别的世界
narration.text: 选中土卫六，读一读探测器发现的特点：它外面包着厚厚的大气，还有液体组成的湖海，不过那些液体不是我们喝的水。再选土卫二：它有明亮的冰壳，还会从南边喷出水汽和冰粒。这些发现来自探测器认真拍照和测量；眼前的圆球只是帮我们找到卫星，不会在图里展开那些地貌或喷流。
narration.cue: 依次选择土卫六与土卫二，阅读对应发现；不切换近景或显示模拟喷流。

narration.label: 读一读真正的大小
narration.text: 最后用直径读数比大小。选中土卫六，记下它的直径，再读土卫二的直径。你会发现，土卫六大得多。画面为了让大家都看得见，分别调整了球体和距离；不能拿屏幕上的圆球或空位当尺子。这些世界有许多值得研究的秘密，但有水的地方，也不能马上说一定住着生命。
narration.cue: 依次选择土卫六和土卫二，对照直径读数；保持轨道图，说明球体与间距不按共同真实比例显示。

en.question: Do differently sized moons around Saturn take the same time to finish an orbit?
en.observe: Open Saturn’s moon view in the Solar System explorer and let the orbit illustration run. Select Mimas and Titan in turn to compare period and diameter readouts. Read the discoveries about Titan and Enceladus, distinguishing screen markers, physical sizes and spacecraft evidence.

academic.title: Different orbits in one gravitational field
academic.body: When Saturn dominates and perturbations are neglected, T²≈4π²a³/(GM), so moons farther out generally have longer periods. The seven selected moons share a simulation clock, but orbital spacing is compressed and bodies enlarged. Real orbits include resonances, eccentricity, and inclination changes. Orbit guides are not material rings, and moons are not beads attached to Saturn’s rings.

academic.title: Very different satellite environments
academic.body: Titan has a thick, mainly nitrogen atmosphere and confirmed surface lakes and seas of methane and ethane. Its liquid cycle is not Earth’s water cycle. Enceladus has a global ocean beneath its ice shell and releases water vapor and icy particles near its south pole. Cassini studied these environments using images, spectra, and particle measurements. Water and organic compounds do not establish the presence of life.

academic.title: Compare diameter readouts
academic.body: Selecting a moon shows its orbital period and diameter. Compare the diameter values with their units: bodies and distances in the orbit view are scaled separately, so the displayed spheres are not a common-length measurement. Titan’s physical diameter is much larger than Enceladus’s. These seven are a teaching selection, not Saturn’s total; complete inventories and counts require a source and date.

en.misconception: Saturn has more than seven moons. Titan’s surface lakes are not liquid water, and Enceladus’s plumes do not prove life has been found.
en.boundary: Circular orbits and illustrative phases simplify motion; body sizes and orbital distances are scaled separately. Moons appear as simplified spheres. Atmospheres, oceans and south-polar plumes are spacecraft discoveries described in text, not close-up surface or plume simulations in this view. There is no common true-scale moon-size workbench; compare the diameter values.

narration.label: Partners beyond the rings
narration.text: Saturn has beautiful rings and many moons nearby. Today we will meet seven of them, but Saturn does not have only seven. Some are large, some small, some nearer, and some farther away. Choose a moon, read its name, and locate it in the picture so you can keep following it.
narration.cue: Select Titan in the orbit overview.

narration.label: Who completes a lap?
narration.text: Let the moons orbit and compare Mimas, farther in, with more distant Titan. Pause and predict: over the same playback interval, which makes more laps? Select each one and read its orbital period. The moons share one Saturn, but they do not travel as a matching parade at one speed. Each has its own rhythm.
narration.cue: Compare Mimas and Titan; pause four seconds.

narration.label: Two unusual worlds
narration.text: Select Titan and read the spacecraft discoveries. It has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid, but that liquid is not the water we drink. Next select Enceladus: it has a bright icy shell and sprays water vapor and icy grains from its southern region. Spacecraft discovered these features with careful pictures and measurements. The spheres help us locate the moons; they do not unfold those landscapes or plumes in the picture.
narration.cue: Select Titan and Enceladus in turn and read their discoveries; do not switch to a close-up or show simulated plumes.

narration.label: Read their physical sizes
narration.text: Finally, compare the diameter readouts. Select Titan and note its diameter, then read Enceladus’s diameter. Titan is much larger. To keep the moons visible, the picture adjusts body sizes and distances separately; its spheres and gaps cannot be used as a ruler. These worlds hold many questions to investigate. Even where there is water, we cannot immediately conclude that something is living there.
narration.cue: Select Titan and Enceladus in turn to compare diameter readouts. Keep the orbit view and explain that spheres and spacing do not share a true length scale.
